# The story so far

## Can we trust our survey?

:::{.callout-tip title="Two Questions"}
Our sleep survey is not perfect. Some students skipped questions, and the caffeine facts live in a different table. 

1. Can we trust our averages when people skip questions? (*Missing values*, Chapter 18)
2. Do students who drink more caffeine sleep less? (*Joins*, Chapter 19)
:::

# Part 1: Missing values


## What are missing values? {.smaller}

| | **Explicit** missing | **Implicit** missing |
|--|---|---|
| Idea | The data has a cell and it says `NA` | The data has no row at all |
| Example from survey | A student left `sleep_hours` blank | Nobody answered between 3 and 4 AM, so that hour is not in the data |
| Another example | `stress_level` left blank | Matcha and Bubble tea: nobody chose them, so they never appear |
| How to see it | `is.na()`, `count()` | Compare with what should be there: `complete()`, `anti_join()` |
| How to fix it | `drop_na()`, `na.rm`, `coalesce()`, `replace_na()` | `complete()` adds the rows |

## A simple example

```{webr}
responses <- tibble(
  day = c("Mon", "Tue", "Thu"),
  n = c(10, NA, 7)
)
responses
```

::: {.callout-caution title="Checkpoint"}
What is the missing data here?
:::

## Example Continued

- **Tuesday** is explicit: the row exists and `n` is `NA`
- **Wednesday** is implicit: there is no row at all

::: {.callout-important title="Plots hide implicit gaps"}
A chart of this table draws Mon, Tue, Thu. Nothing on the plot says that Wednesday is missing.
:::

## Brief Review of `NA`

:::{.callout-note title="`NA` is contagious"}
An unknown value makes almost every answer unknown.
- E.g. arithemtic like addition/subtraction
- E.g. statistics like mean/median)
:::

```{webr}
NA > 5
NA == NA
NA + 10
mean(c(4, NA, 6))
mean(c(4, NA, 6), na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Testing for `NA`

:::{.callout-warning title="What do we do?"}
`NA == NA` is `NA`, so we can use `is.na()` to test for it
:::

```{webr}
x <- c(4, NA, 6)
is.na(x)
```

## Filtering

:::{.callout-tip title="Try running the following code"}
Suppose that I collected these sleep survey response from 1000 students. I want to filter and count the number of students that sleep less than 6 hours on average, and then count the number of students that sleep for greater or equal to 6 hours per night. What are the results showing me?
:::

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(sleep_hours < 6) |>
  nrow()

survey |>
  filter(sleep_hours >= 6) |>
  nrow()
```


---

![](https://encrypted-tbn0.gstatic.com/images?q=tbn:ANd9GcQD6zBaE0CPck8lDLhzu74scDYkOFoPZ11cfjF4WXF5ww&s=10){.r-stretch fig-align="center"}

---

## The `filter()` trap

::: {.callout-caution}
The two counts do **not** add up to 1000! `filter()` drops rows where the condition is `NA`. Missing students vanish from **both** sides. So how many students did not had `NA` in the survey response?
:::

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(is.na(sleep_hours)) |>
  nrow()
```

## How much is missing?

Count the `NA`s in every column at once with `across()`:

```{webr}
survey |>
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "question", values_to = "missing") |>
  filter(missing > 0)
```

- `.x` stands for "the current column"
- `bedtime` shows 23: the truly blank answers

## Blank vs `NA`

An empty cell is not always `NA`. It depends on how the file is read:

```{webr}
raw <- read.csv("data/sleep_survey_v2.csv", na.strings = character(),
                fileEncoding = "WINDOWS-1252")
raw |>
  summarize(
    blank_text = sum(bedtime == ""),
    real_na = sum(is.na(bedtime))
  )
```

::: {.callout-warning title="No error, no warning"}
With `na.strings = character()`, the 23 blanks become **empty text**, and `is.na()` finds none of them. The `na.strings` argument tells `read.csv()` which strings mean "missing". We used `na.strings = c("", "NA")`.
:::

## Missing in disguise

What about `idk`, `varies` and `n/a`? They are not blank, but they carry **no information**:

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(!str_detect(bedtime, regex("\\d|midnight", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  count(bedtime, sort = TRUE)
```

- We can use `regex` (regular expressions) from Lecture 10 to find them: i.e. no digit, and not `midnight`.
- Decide what counts as missing, and write it down

## Turn them into `NA`

```{webr}
#| autorun: TRUE
survey <- survey |>
  mutate(
    bedtime = if_else(
      str_detect(bedtime, regex("\\d|midnight", ignore_case = TRUE)),
      bedtime, NA_character_
    )
  )

survey |>
  summarize(missing_bedtimes = sum(is.na(bedtime)))
```

- From 23 blanks to **57** unusable answers: now they are explicit missing values

## A representation for `NA`?

:::{.callout-note title="`na_if()`"}
This function allows you to transform a *single* value that implies *missing* (e.g an extreme value like `-99`), and turn it into `NA`.
:::

```{webr}
scores <- c(72, -99, 85, -99, 90)
scores_new <- na_if(scores, -99)

mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
mean(scores_new, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## Does the missing matter?

::: {.callout-tip title=""}
Suppose that you want to compare students who answered with students who did not. Did the *missing data* affect your results?
:::

```{webr}
survey |>
  group_by(stress_missing = is.na(stress_level)) |>
  summarize(students = n(), mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE))

survey |>
  group_by(grade_missing = is.na(avg_grade)) |>
  summarize(students = n(), mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE))
```


## Observations

:::{.callout-tip title="missing looks *random*"}
The averages are close, and the missing groups are small (a few dozen students)
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Random is not guaranteed"}
If stressed students skip the stress question, dropping them makes everyone look calmer. Always ask **who** is missing, not just **how many**.
:::

## Handling missing values

| Tool | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `na.rm = TRUE` | Ignore the `NA`s inside one calculation |
| `drop_na()` | Remove the **rows** that have `NA` |
| `replace_na()` | Replace `NA` with a value you choose |
| `coalesce()` | Take the first value that is not `NA` |

```{webr}
survey |>
  mutate(drink = replace_na(favourite_drink, "No answer")) |>
  count(drink, sort = TRUE)
```

## Different ways to find the mean

```{webr}
bind_rows(
  # 1) Ignore those that did not answer sleep_hours.
  survey |>
    summarize(method = "na.rm = TRUE", students = sum(!is.na(sleep_hours)),
              mean = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE)),
  # 2) Drop all NA's in three variables.
  survey |>
    drop_na(sleep_hours, stress_level, avg_grade) |>
    summarize(method = "drop_na() on 3 columns", students = n(),
              mean = mean(sleep_hours), sd = sd(sleep_hours)),
  # 3) Imputation: give these missing values a "mean-value"
  survey |>
    mutate(sleep_hours = replace_na(sleep_hours, mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
    summarize(method = "fill with the mean", students = n(),
              mean = mean(sleep_hours), sd = sd(sleep_hours))
)
```

## Imputation

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
Imputation means filling in a missing value with an estimate. 

- **Fixed value**: a number you choose, such as `0`
- **Mean**: the average of the answers we have (**mean imputation**)
- **Last value**: the last known value above it
:::

::: {.callout-important title="It comes with a cost"}
Filling with the mean keeps the average but shrinks the spread (`sd`), and it makes 35 students look more typical than they are. Dropping rows loses students. There is no free option, so choose, and say which.
:::

Work with the five questions `sleep_hours`, `stress_level`, `favourite_drink`, `has_early_class` and `avg_grade`.

#| exercise: ex_missing

## When did the students respond to the survey?

:::{.callout-tip title="Implicit missing"}
When we show a (line) plot, the lines connect the hours before and after each gap. So in fact, it hides the hours (timeslot) when nobody answered in the survey.
:::

```{webr}
per_hour <- survey |>
  mutate(survey_date = parse_date_time(
    survey_date,
    orders = c("ymd HMS", "ymd HM", "mdy HMS", "mdy HM"),
    tz = "America/Toronto"
  )) |>
  mutate(hour_bin = floor_date(survey_date, "hour")) |>
  count(hour_bin)

per_hour |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour_bin, y = n)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Responses per hour", x = NULL, y = "Responses") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```


## Filling in the missing rows

:::{.callout-note title="`complete()`"}
This function adds the rows that are missing from a table. You tell it which values should exist, and it creates a row for every one that’s absent, and `fill` the other columns with `NA` or a value that you choose.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: TRUE
per_hour_full <- per_hour |>
  complete(
    hour_bin = seq(min(hour_bin), max(hour_bin), by = "hour"),
    fill = list(n = 0)
  )

per_hour_full |>
  count(empty_hour = n == 0)
```


## Now the gaps are filled in

```{webr}
per_hour_full |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hour_bin, y = n)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = n == 0), show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "black", "TRUE" = "firebrick")) +
  labs(
    title = "Responses per hour, with the empty hours in red",
    x = NULL, y = "Responses"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

- The red points are the nights when nobody was answering the survey
- The line now dips to zero, which is what really happened

## Empty groups

A group with **no rows** is also implicit missing. `group_by(.drop = FALSE)` keeps every level of a factor:

```{webr}
survey |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  mutate(favourite_drink = factor(favourite_drink, levels = drinks$drink)) |>
  group_by(favourite_drink, .drop = FALSE) |>
  summarize(students = n())
```

- Without `.drop = FALSE`, Matcha and Bubble tea would not appear at all
- When we learned about "Factors" from last week, we know that we should keep track of the levels that **should** be there

counts <- tibble(

  n = c(257, NA, 149, 144)
)

counts |>

# Part 2: Joins

## Does caffeine cost us sleep?

```{r echo=FALSE}
#| context: output
#| autorun: true
survey |>
  left_join(drinks, by = join_by(favourite_drink == drink)) |>
  filter(!is.na(caffeine_mg)) |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(mean_caffeine = mean(caffeine_mg)) |>
  mutate(program = fct_reorder(program, mean_caffeine)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_caffeine, y = program)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste(round(mean_caffeine), "mg")), hjust = -0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
  labs(
    title = "Average caffeine in a student's favourite drink",
    x = "Caffeine (mg)", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```


## Answering one question using two tables

| Step | Tool (Chapter 19) |
|------|-------------------|
| Find the matching column | *Keys*: `favourite_drink` and `drink` |
| Add columns from another table | `left_join()`, `join_by()` |
| Other ways to combine | `inner_join()`, `full_join()` |
| Check what did not match | `anti_join()`, `semi_join()` |

## The two tables

```{webr}
survey |>
  select(student_id, favourite_drink) |>
  head(5)

drinks
```

- The survey has the drink name, and the drinks table has the facts
- The shared information is the drink name: that is the **key**



## Keys

:::{.callout-note title="Primary Key"}
A primary key is a column whose values are unique: no two rows share one, so each value picks out exactly one row. E.g.

  - `student_id` in `survey`: each ID is one student
  - The `drink` column in the `drinks` table: "Coffee" appears in one row only

:::


:::{.callout-tip title="Foreign Key"}
 A foreign key is a column in another table that holds those same values.
  - `favourite_drink` in `survey` holds drink names like "Coffee"
  - Many students can share the same favourite drink like coffee

:::


## Combining tables

:::{.callout-note title="`left_join()`"}
The function `left_join(x, y)` keeps every row of `x` and adds the matching columns of `y`. In the end, you will get the same number of rows but more columns (more information you learn about each observation). 

- You can also use `join_by(a == b)` to say which column in `x` matches with which column in `y`

:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: TRUE
# Combine the tables
survey_drinks <- survey |>
  left_join(drinks, by = join_by(favourite_drink == drink))
# Showing first 8 rows
survey_drinks |>
  select(student_id, favourite_drink, serving_ml, caffeine_mg, sugary) |>
  head(8)
```


## What about students with no drink?

```{webr}
survey_drinks |>
  filter(is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  select(student_id, favourite_drink, caffeine_mg) 


survey_drinks |>
  summarize(missing_caffeine = sum(is.na(caffeine_mg)))
```

- No drink means no match, so `caffeine_mg` is `NA`
- This is Part 1 again: explicit missing, created by the join

## Sleep and caffeine

```r
survey_drinks |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  group_by(favourite_drink, caffeine_mg) |>
  summarize(mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(favourite_drink = fct_reorder(favourite_drink, mean_sleep)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_sleep, y = favourite_drink)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(mean_sleep, 1), " h  (", caffeine_mg, " mg)")),
    hjust = -0.1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.3))) +
  labs(
    title = "Average sleep by favourite drink, with its caffeine",
    x = "Average hours of sleep", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

## Is this what you expected?

```{r echo=FALSE}
survey_drinks |>
  filter(!is.na(favourite_drink)) |>
  group_by(favourite_drink, caffeine_mg) |>
  summarize(mean_sleep = mean(sleep_hours, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(favourite_drink = fct_reorder(favourite_drink, mean_sleep)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_sleep, y = favourite_drink)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(mean_sleep, 1), " h  (", caffeine_mg, " mg)")),
    hjust = -0.1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.3))) +
  labs(
    title = "Average sleep by favourite drink, with its caffeine",
    x = "Average hours of sleep", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Association, not cause"}
Students who drink energy drinks also differ in workload and program. The chart shows a pattern, not what causes it.
:::

## Different types of "joins"

```{webr}
x <- tibble(key = c(1, 2, 3), x_value = c("a", "b", "c"))
y <- tibble(key = c(1, 2, 4), y_value = c("A", "B", "D"))

inner_join(x, y, by = "key")
left_join(x, y, by = "key")
full_join(x, y, by = "key")
```

| Join | What The Table Keeps |
|------|-------|
| `inner_join()` | Only rows with a match in both |
| `left_join()` | All rows of `x`, plus matches from `y` |
| `full_join()` | All rows of both |


## Filtering joins

:::{.callout-warning title="Who did not match?"}
`anti_join()` keeps the rows of `x` with **no match** in `y`. 

`semi_join()` keeps the rows **with** a match.
:::

```{webr}
# Drinks that no student chose
drinks |>
  anti_join(survey, by = join_by(drink == favourite_drink))

# Students whose drink is not in the drinks table
survey |>
  anti_join(drinks, by = join_by(favourite_drink == drink)) |>
  count(favourite_drink)

# Students whose drink is in the drinks table
survey |>
  semi_join(drinks, by = join_by(favourite_drink == drink)) |>
  nrow()
```


## What changed?

::: {.callout-important title="Using Joins to find implicit missing"}
Matcha and Bubble tea were never in the survey: **implicit** missing. Filtering joins *did not add any columns*. They only filter rows.
:::

```{webr}
survey |>
  anti_join(drinks, by = join_by(favourite_drink == drink))
```

## Caffeine by early class

```r
survey_drinks |>
  filter(!is.na(has_early_class), !is.na(caffeine_mg)) |>
  mutate(group = if_else(has_early_class == "Yes", "Early class", "No early class")) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarize(mean_caffeine = mean(caffeine_mg)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mean_caffeine, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste(round(mean_caffeine), "mg")), hjust = -0.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
  labs(
    title = "Early-class students pick stronger drinks",
    x = "Average caffeine (mg)", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
```

## Exercise 3

::: {.callout-tip title="Live exercise"}
1. Join `drinks` to the survey and compute the proportion of students who chose a sugary drink, for each program. Ignore students with no drink.
2. How many students chose a drink that has more than 100 mg of caffeine?
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_joins
# Part 1
survey |>
  left_join(drinks, by = join_by()) |>
  filter(!is.na(sugary)) |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(share_sugary = )

# Part 2
survey |>
  left_join(drinks, by = join_by()) |>
  filter() |>
  nrow()
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_joins
#| solution: true
# Part 1: the mean of a logical vector is a proportion
survey |>
  left_join(drinks, by = join_by(favourite_drink == drink)) |>
  filter(!is.na(sugary)) |>
  group_by(program) |>
  summarize(share_sugary = mean(sugary == "Yes"))

# Part 2: only the energy drink has more than 100 mg
survey |>
  left_join(drinks, by = join_by(favourite_drink == drink)) |>
  filter(caffeine_mg > 100) |>
  nrow()
```

# Appendix: read the text


## Missing values: other tools (i) {.smaller}

| Tool | What it does | Tiny example | Read the section on |
|------|--------------|--------------|---------------------|
| `fill()` | Fills `NA`s with the last value above (or below) | `fill(df, n, .direction = "down")` | Last observation carried forward |
| `coalesce()` | First value that is not `NA` | `coalesce(x, 0)` | Fixed values |
| `NaN`, `is.nan()` | "Not a number", for example `0 / 0` | `is.nan(0 / 0)` | NaN |
| `drop_na()` with columns | Drops only rows missing **those** columns | `drop_na(df, avg_grade)` | Explicit missing values |


## Missing values: other tools (ii) {.smaller}

| Tool | What it does | Tiny example | Read the section on |
|------|--------------|--------------|---------------------|
| `if_any()`, `if_all()` | Tests a condition across several columns | `filter(if_any(a:c, is.na))` | Explicit missing values |
| `complete()` with `nesting()` | Adds only the combinations that make sense | `complete(df, nesting(a, b))` | Implicit missing values |
| `anti_join()` | Finds implicit gaps by comparing with a full list | `anti_join(all_days, df)` | Implicit missing values |


## Missing values: other tools (iii) {.smaller}

| Tool | What it does | Tiny example | Read the section on |
|------|--------------|--------------|---------------------|
| `.drop = FALSE` | Keeps empty groups in `group_by()` | `group_by(f, .drop = FALSE)` | Factors and empty groups |
| `scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE)` | Keeps empty levels on a plot axis | `scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE)` | Factors and empty groups |


## Joins: other tools (i) {.smaller}

| Tool | What it does | Tiny example | Read the section on |
|------|--------------|--------------|---------------------|
| `right_join()` | Keeps **all** rows of `y` | `right_join(x, y, by = "key")` | Mutating joins |
| `by = join_by(a == b)` | Matches columns with different names | `join_by(drink == favourite_drink)` | Specifying join keys |
| `suffix` | Renames columns with the same name | `left_join(x, y, suffix = c("_x", "_y"))` | Specifying join keys |
| `relationship`, `multiple` | Checks and controls many-to-many matches | `left_join(x, y, relationship = "many-to-one")` | How do joins work? |
| `unmatched = "error"` | Stops if a row has no match | `inner_join(x, y, unmatched = "error")` | Specifying join keys |



## Joins: other tools (ii) {.smaller}

| Tool | What it does | Tiny example | Read the section on |
|------|--------------|--------------|---------------------|
| `cross_join()` | Every row of `x` with every row of `y` | `cross_join(x, y)` | Cross joins |
| Inequality joins | Match with `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | `join_by(date >= start)` | Filtering joins |
| Rolling joins | Match with the **closest** value | `join_by(closest(date >= start))` | Rolling joins |
| Overlap joins | Match ranges that overlap | `join_by(overlaps(a, b, c, d))` | Overlap joins |
| Surrogate keys | A made-up key, such as `row_number()` | `mutate(id = row_number())` | Primary and foreign keys |
